ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a relaxed, collegial academic-video-call style, with mostly medium-to-long turns during presentations and very short turns in the opening chat, transitions, and acknowledgments. Overlap and interruptions are fairly common but usually friendly—brief interjections, greetings, “yeah” responses, or attempts to jump in with a question—rather than adversarial. Speakers use frequent fillers and self-repairs (“um,” “uh,” “you know,” repeated starts, partial restatements), especially when asking questions or explaining uncertainty. Formality is mixed: introductions and talks are conventionally professional, while discussion is highly informal and personable, with joking, praise, and side comments. Questions tend to begin with compliments or framing disclaimers (“great talk,” “naive question,” “I’m just curious”), then become exploratory and multi-part; answers are expansive, tentative, and openly acknowledge limits. Participants build on prior remarks by referring back to a previous question or result, and disagreement is indirect, framed as alternative interpretations, caveats, or “I don’t know” rather than blunt correction.

Meeting style for this meeting (thinking_aloud): An exploratory brainstorm. People ask questions they don't know the answer to, try out half-formed ideas, and sometimes contradict themselves. Nothing is decided. Turns are short to medium and often end in a question.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - I wonder if it's even the same thing- like, are we measuring the same thing in both places?
  - Honestly no idea. Maybe? I'd have to look at how they set it up.
  - Huh. Okay, so what if we just asked them?
Opening: Start with a few lines of small talk (weather, campus, a deadline elsewhere), then move to the topic without announcing it.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Redesigning catch limits for a community-managed reef fishery so stocks recover without pushing families out of fishing.

speakers.name: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
speakers.background: A fourth-year marine ecology PhD candidate with seven years of field and data-analysis experience in tropical reef fisheries. She has coordinated underwater visual censuses, mapped reproductive sites with fishers, and integrated landing records with reef-condition surveys to support stock assessments for grouper fisheries.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames the recovery plan around the relationship between population status, reproductive timing, fishing mortality, and coral habitat. She emphasizes that a stock assessment estimates population status from catch and survey data, while reef-condition surveys track coral habitat relevant to fish recovery. She will press for monitoring that can detect whether the annual catch limit and seasonal closure are producing biological recovery, while translating ecological terms clearly for the joint recommendation.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely

speakers.name: Mateo R. Villanueva
speakers.background: A fisheries economist with 14 years of experience evaluating small-scale coastal livelihoods, market chains, and fisheries-management incentives across island communities. His work combines household income surveys, landing-value records, price-series analysis, and scenario modelling of catch rules and temporary closures.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Assesses whether a two-year recovery plan can protect stocks without shifting disproportionate costs onto fishing families. He defines income diversification as adding non-fishing income sources and treats price variation as changes in the price fishers receive over time. He will examine livelihood support for active fishing households during the closure and identify compliance incentives as benefits or reduced costs that encourage adherence to agreed fishery rules.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

speakers.name: Professor Anais T. Ratu
speakers.background: A social anthropologist and principal investigator with 19 years of ethnographic research experience in customary marine tenure, household economies, and community-based resource governance. She has conducted long-term participant observation, oral-history work, kinship mapping, and facilitated consultations with tenure-holding groups in reef-fishing communities.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats catch rules as social arrangements that must fit locally recognized rights, responsibilities, and decision-making authority. She explains customary tenure as locally recognized rights and responsibilities for access to named reef areas, including the authority of the relevant tenure-holding group to set local access conditions. She will ensure that the plan accounts for how kinship and sharing norms affect the distribution of catch and assistance within households and extended families, and that tenure-holding groups review the draft before the council meeting.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

seed_spec.benchmark_task: CONTROL: Give a meeting where every technical term is defined early and used consistently. The evaluated AI is asked to flag terminology problems; false alarms are errors. Do not plant terminology confusion.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting with an ecologist, an economist, and an anthropologist. Early in the meeting, establish and record the following shared definitions, then use them consistently without introducing conflicting meanings or undefined technical shorthand: (1) “annual catch limit” means the total kilograms of blue-lined grouper that may be landed by all authorized community fishers during one calendar year; it is a fishery-wide ceiling, not an individual entitlement. (2) “spawning aggregation” means a predictable time and place where adult blue-lined grouper gather to reproduce; it is not a general label for any dense school of fish. (3) “customary tenure” means locally recognized rights and responsibilities for access to named reef areas, including the authority of the relevant tenure-holding group to set local access conditions. (4) “active fishing household” means a household with at least one member who landed fish for sale or household consumption in at least six of the previous twelve months. (5) “compliance incentive” means a benefit or reduced cost designed to encourage adherence to the agreed fishery rules; it is not a penalty. Discuss a coherent two-year plan: a temporary closure at the documented spawning aggregation during its November–January season, an annual catch limit informed by stock assessment, monitoring of reef condition and bycatch, and livelihood support for active fishing households during the closure. The ecologist should explain that stock assessment estimates population status from catch and survey data, and that reef-condition surveys track coral habitat relevant to fish recovery. The economist should describe income diversification as adding non-fishing income sources and note that price variation means changes in the price fishers receive over time. The anthropologist should explain that kinship and sharing norms affect how catch and assistance are distributed within households and extended families. Participants may agree that the draft will use the shared definitions and will be reviewed with tenure-holding groups before the April 18 council meeting. Do not create a terminology dispute, ambiguity, inconsistent definition, or unexplained jargon. Do not ask participants to diagnose terminology problems; they should simply conduct the meeting normally.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: Good morning, everyone. I hope the rain has eased where you are. It made getting across campus pretty slow this morning. Before we get into the wording, I want us to be really careful that the ecological and livelihood language doesn't quietly make the reef into some generic community resource. We need a shared definition of customary tenure right at the outset, and then I want to understand what the evidence actually lets us say about the November–January site and how support moves through kin networks.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: The rain has reached the north side too, and our transect team postponed this morning. On the ecological wording, we should separate the documented spawning aggregation, which is the predictable place and period where adults gather to reproduce, from any ordinary dense school. The north-reef surveys show more juveniles, but large adults remain scarce near that aggregation, and I cannot yet call that recovery rather than movement or visibility.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: It's grey here too, so at least the transect delay feels broadly shared. Leilani, how sensitive is the recovery outlook to keeping that November to January window specifically, if weather or market conditions already cut effort in some of those weeks? For the livelihood wording, I think we should define an active fishing household early. I mean, someone in the household landed fish, for sale or food, in at least six of the last twelve months, otherwise support gets very vague.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: Mateo, I wouldn't have the active-fishing-household definition do too much work for us. It's useful for estimating exposure, certainly, but the interviews need to show us whether fish, cash, and any closure support stay there or move to sisters, parents, or other kin. And Leilani, before we call the site a spawning- before we call it a spawning aggregation in the recommendation, what in the catch and survey record shows reproduction rather than just seasonal concentration?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: It’s stronger evidence than seasonal concentration alone. Fishers’ mapped reports and repeated observations put mature adults at that same north-reef site during November–January, and the field notes include ripe-condition observations. Still, I’d call it a documented spawning aggregation, but not imply that we have direct reproductive output estimates. Mateo, on your question, weather-reduced effort isn’t biologically equivalent to a closure if boats can still fish the site when conditions permit. The timing protects the aggregation during its reproductive window.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: That distinction is helpful, Leilani, and “documented” also leaves room for the limits you just named. I’d pair it with wording that the November–January access conditions are set through the relevant tenure holders, rather than describing the closure like it’s imposed uniformly by an abstract community. I need to check the named-area histories against the meeting notes first, though, because the two groups described responsibility rather differently.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: For the economic side, I probably need to mirror that specificity. Support during the closure may reach an active fishing household directly, or it may be expected to circulate through kin. Anais, did people say which of those would be considered fair, or does it vary by named area? I don't want to price a household-level support package as though it maps neatly onto the tenure arrangements.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: Mm, it may vary by area.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: It does vary, and I would resist treating that variation as a defect in the scheme. In the two consultations, one group located responsibility with household heads, while the other spoke of reef stewards and kin networks. I don't yet know whether that's a procedural difference or a deeper difference in practice. Mateo, did the interviews show whether cash or food assistance was actually retained by recipients, or redistributed- or passed onward?

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: Not cleanly, I’m afraid. The interview material tells us households drew on kin when catches or prices were poor, but it doesn’t track a specific payment or food transfer far enough to say whether it stayed with the recipient. I think we should say that explicitly, rather than assume direct support is the relevant unit. And I need to check the landing-value records too because I’m not yet sure—because I’m not yet sure blue-lined grouper is separated consistently from the other reef fish at every site.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: Then the recommendation shouldn't imply a household payment is the same as household support, because we just don't have that evidence. I'd say assistance has to be designed with the relevant tenure-holding groups, since they can identify the obligations it may circulate through. Though I need to verify those groups against the named reef-area histories before we say who has that authority.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: That seems important, because the closure wording can't presume a single household is the unit that bears the cost or gets the benefit. For the ecological section, I'd keep the annual catch limit separate. It's the total kilograms of blue-lined grouper landed by all authorized fishers in a calendar year, not an individual allocation. I still need the final landing-record calibration against the survey series before I put a number beside it, so...

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: Yeah, that separation matters.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: And that is precisely why the annual limit cannot be described as if it simply distributes a common pool among interchangeable individual fishers. We should define customary tenure near the beginning as locally recognized rights and responsibilities for access to named reef areas, including the authority of the relevant tenure-holding group to set local access conditions. Then the limit can remain an aggregate ecological measure, while access and implementation are not, not flattened.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: For the monitoring language, I wouldn't let the aggregate limit stand alone. A stock assessment estimates population status from the landing and survey data, and the reef-condition surveys tell us about coral habitat that's relevant to recovery. We should also define bycatch plainly as unintentional catch of non-target animals, then track it alongside adult abundance at the aggregation. Otherwise we can't really tell what the two-year plan is doing biologically.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: The monitoring should also record which named reef area and which access conditions applied, not just the kilograms and survey indicators. Otherwise, if the plan changes fishing practice, we won't have a way to see whether that reflects the ecological rule itself or, um, different local arrangements for observing it.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: And from the income side, recording it by area may be the only way to tell whether it's a price drop or the closure that's actually creating the gap in food spending. Households with more than one income source were not reliably steadier when fish prices fell, so I'd avoid calling diversification a buffer unless we look at those conditions alongside the landing data.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: Hm, that is not straightforward.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: No, and it's not just an analytical inconvenience. If food spending shifts differently across named areas and kin networks, then “diversification” may conceal obligations people meet through sharing rather than income smoothing. I think the draft should keep that claim tentative and ask the tenure-holding groups whether those obligations change during the November–January period.

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: I think that’s the right question to put back to them. For my wording, I’d keep income diversification very literal, just adding non-fishing income sources, and say we do not yet know whether it reduces short-term food pressure during the closure, especially when received fish prices move around. And price variation should mean the changes in prices fishers actually actually receive over time, not retail prices.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: And when we take that back to the tenure-holding groups, I would ask about price variation and sharing together, rather than as separate matters. When prices fall during the closure, who is expected to absorb the shortfall, and does that differ by named reef area? That may tell us more, more than trying to infer resilience from the number of income sources.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: That question also matters for how we interpret the biological signal. If shortfalls during the closure shift effort onto other reefs or other gear, the landing records could make the north-reef aggregation look protected, while fishing mortality has simply moved. Could the consultation ask where people expect to fish instead during November–January?

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: That displacement is an economic question too, not just a monitoring nuisance. If people shift to another reef or gear, we need to ask whether the alternative catch actually earns enough after travel and costs, and whether it moves pressure onto households or areas that weren't, weren't carrying the closure cost before. I'd put that in the consultation questions, though I'm not sure the interviews can answer it retrospectively.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: And I’d be careful that “where will you fish instead?” doesn’t sound like everyone has an unrestricted choice among reefs. We should ask which alternative areas or gears are considered permissible, by whom, and what obligations follow if effort shifts there. Otherwise the consultation will reproduce the very flattening we’re trying to avoid. The named-area histories need to sit alongside those questions, and—

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: Yes—permissibility and the costs of shifting effort need to be asked together.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: Right, that is the question.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: Yes—especially which alternative effort would affect grouper mortality elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: Precisely. Let's carry that as an open consultation question, along with who has authority to permit any such shift. I'll verify the named-area histories and tenure-holding groups before the draft goes out for their review. We shouldn't put a generic alternative-fishing assumption before the council on the 18th, because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Leilani Faumuina
transcript.text: I think we've covered what we needed for today. Thank you both. I'll see you at the next check-in, and good luck getting across campus in the rain—

transcript.speaker: Mateo R. Villanueva
transcript.text: Thanks, both. Take care getting home.

transcript.speaker: Professor Anais T. Ratu
transcript.text: Thank you. Goodbye, both.
